newsitem.title: USA: Author le Carre blasts New York Times review.
newsitem.headline: Author le Carre blasts New York Times review.

text.p: Best-selling British author John le Carre criticized New York Times Book Review editors on Sunday in a New York appearance promoting his new novel, "The Tailor of Panama."

After answering questions at the 92nd Street Y from Paris Review editor George Plimpton, as part of a program entitled "The Paris Review Writers-at-Work," le Carre interrupted a reading from the work to protest against the newspaper's book reviewer in its Sunday edition, who seemed to be accusing him of anti-Semitism.

The review, specifically, said that le Carre's fictional character, Harry Pendel, a London Jew transplanted to Panama, "however little Mr. le Carre intended it, (is) yet another literary avatar of Judas."

The reviewer writes of his "unease" over Pendel's background, mentioning Pendel's uncle who was a tailor to the Nazis. "As you read, the phrase 'rootless cosmopolitans' scratches at the doors of your mind," the review said.

The New York Times review was written by Norman Rush, identified as the author of "Whites" and "Mating" and working on a new novel, "Mortals." Le Carre did not identify the reviewer by name but criticized the paper.
"I blame the New York Times" for allowing that passage to run, le Carre said. "I've had a lot of tomatoes thrown at me, but this one missed."

Because of his experience and work background for the British Foreign Service in eastern Europe and his writing in earlier novels, he had always been aware of Jewish sensitivities, the author said, adding, "I have a completely clean record."

When le Carre, author of "The Little Drummer Girl," "Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy" and other best-selling Cold War spy novels, completed his impromptu defense, the audience at the Jewish center applauded loudly.
